Why a second app is needed at all

CloudSaver never uploads anything: it holds no internet permission, so there is no code in it that could. What it does is make a smaller copy of each photo and video and put it in one folder. Your cloud app uploads that folder. Two apps, one job each \u2014 and because the upload is not ours, your files reach your cloud exactly as that cloud normally receives them, with its own encryption and its own account.

Any app that can be told to back up one folder you choose. End-to-end encrypted apps suit it best, because they store what you send without making it smaller themselves \u2014 so the saving CloudSaver made is the saving you keep. Apps that already shrink photos on their own servers gain far less from this, which is why they are listed but not recommended.

In your cloud app, turn auto-backup on for the CloudSaver folder and off for your camera folder. Backing up both stores every photo twice \u2014 once full size, once optimised \u2014 and fills the plan faster than using no CloudSaver at all. This is the single most expensive mistake available here, which is why setup shows it before anything runs.
How the app knows which one you use

It looks for the cloud apps it knows and picks the one it finds. If you install one later it is found on the next time you open CloudSaver, and the change is written into Activity so you can see it happened. You can always set it yourself in Settings; a choice you made is never overwritten while that app is still on the phone.
What the choice is actually used for

Proof. Before any original can be offered for removal, CloudSaver has to be satisfied that the copy reached your cloud, and it has two ways to tell. The copy vanishing from the folder is the strong one and needs no help. The other measures how much data your cloud app sent while a copy was waiting, and that needs to know which app to measure \u2014 which is the whole reason the app is named. Get it wrong and nothing breaks: the proof is simply weaker, and the app waits longer before offering anything.
If you have no cloud app

Everything still runs. Photos are optimised on the usual schedule and the copies wait in the folder, using the space you allowed the app. Once that space is full it stops making more and says so on Home. No original is ever offered for removal, because nothing can prove anything reached a cloud. Install an app whenever you like and point it at the folder \u2014 the waiting copies go up on its next backup and nothing is redone.

Change it in Settings and CloudSaver carries on from where it is. Files already proved to have reached the old cloud are not sent again \u2014 they are finished, and re-sending them would put second copies in the new one. Anything still waiting is simply collected by whichever app is now watching the folder.

Two apps do the job: CloudSaver makes the smaller copies and puts them in one folder; the cloud app you already use uploads that folder. CloudSaver never uploads anything and never deletes an original on its own.
No cloud app found on this phone

CloudSaver will still optimise your photos and videos on its usual schedule, and the smaller copies will wait in the Pictures/CloudSaver folder. Nothing is uploaded until you install a cloud app and point it at that folder, and until something collects them the copies use the space you allowed and no original can be offered for removal. You can finish setup now and install a cloud app whenever you like.
What the app stores, and what it never does.

End-to-end encrypted cloud apps keep your photos private, but they upload exactly what you hand them — almost none of them make a file smaller first. So a library of 4K video fills a paid plan quickly, and the only answer usually on offer is to buy more storage every year.

CloudSaver is the step in between. It optimises your photos and videos on the phone itself, into one folder your cloud app already knows how to back up, so the same library reaches your cloud in a fraction of the space — a free or small plan goes a great deal further, and you keep the encrypted app you chose rather than the one with the best price.

It looks after the phone as well as the plan: it works only while the phone is charging, cool and idle, keeps the free space you asked it to keep, finds duplicate files and your largest ones, and never removes an original unless you confirm it yourself.
Works entirely on your phone. No account, no ads, and no internet permission at all.

resources.string: %1$d no longer qualified and were left alone (%2$s).

It makes a smaller copy of each photo and video in the albums you chose, and puts those copies in one folder on your phone. You point your own cloud app at that folder, so only the small copies get uploaded and your cloud plan lasts much longer. Your originals stay exactly where they are, untouched. Everything happens on the phone: CloudSaver has no internet permission and cannot upload anything itself.
Where do the optimised copies go, and what do I select in my cloud app?

They go to Pictures/CloudSaver. If you switch to separate folders in Settings, they go to Pictures/CloudSaver/Photos and Pictures/CloudSaver/Videos instead. In your cloud app, open its backup or folder settings and select that folder \u2014 and turn off backup for DCIM and Camera, or you will be uploading the big originals as well. The Storage screen prints the exact path with a copy button. The folder also appears as an album in your gallery while files wait to be collected \u2014 that is what lets your cloud app see it. Most gallery apps can hide an album from their own settings. CloudSaver never hides it itself, because that would hide it from your cloud app too. One more thing: anything you put into the folder yourself is left exactly where it is \u2014 CloudSaver never moves, renames or removes a file it did not create \u2014 but your cloud app will upload it at full size, so Home shows a note whenever that happens.

No. CloudSaver never edits, moves or deletes an original by itself, at any point, for any reason. The only way an original is ever removed is if you open Free up space, select files yourself, and confirm Android\'s own deletion dialog. On Android 11 and newer it goes to your gallery trash first, where it stays about 30 days; on Android 10 there is no media trash, so Android removes it straight away and says so in its own dialog.

On the default setting, a 12-megapixel photo comes out about 30% smaller with no difference you can see on a phone. Photos above 16 megapixels come down to 16, saving about 75%. Video is capped at 1080p and comes out 60\u201375% smaller, keeping close to the original at normal viewing size. Higher and lower settings are in Settings under Quality, and the app shows what it actually measured on your own files.
Are dates, locations and file names kept?

Yes. Every copy carries the original\'s shooting date and camera details, and the file date is set to match. The GPS location comes too, as long as you allowed the location request during setup \u2014 Android hands apps a copy with the location removed unless that one is granted. Everything else is carried either way. That is why the copies land in the right place chronologically in your cloud instead of all appearing as today. The file name keeps the original name with a short code added, so a copy can always be matched back to its original.
How does CloudSaver know a file reached my cloud?

Two ways, both watched automatically. Some cloud apps delete their own copy after uploading it; when one disappears from the folder and CloudSaver did not remove it, that is proof. Otherwise CloudSaver adds copies a few at a time and watches how many bytes your cloud app sends, so a matching amount right after one file goes out is proof for that file. Every file shows which of the two applies to it, in plain words, and files with no proof are never offered for removal. The daily limit in Settings controls how much CloudSaver adds to the upload folder each day \u2014 which is what your cloud app then uploads. CloudSaver cannot control when that app uploads or which network it uses; set that inside the app itself.
What if my cloud app makes duplicates?

CloudSaver keeps a permanent record of every copy that reached your cloud, matched by content rather than by name. Once a file is on that list it is never sent again, even if you clear the app\'s data or reinstall it. If your phone itself holds the same photo twice, Find space shows those groups and optimises the file only once \u2014 the extras are marked as already handled, not treated as problems. And if your cloud app downloads a copy back to your phone \u2014 into Download or any album \u2014 CloudSaver recognises its own copies by their names and never optimises or re-sends them.
Someone deleted a file from the CloudSaver folder \u2014 what now?

If CloudSaver had already confirmed that file reached your cloud, nothing happens: the disappearance is exactly what an upload looks like, and the original was never at risk. If it had not been confirmed, CloudSaver treats the copy as lost and simply makes it again on the next run. Either way your original is untouched, because the app only ever removes an original after you confirm it yourself.
What about HEIC, RAW, GIF and motion photos?

HEIC photos are converted to JPEG and made smaller like any other photo. RAW, GIF and similar formats are copied exactly as they are, because optimising them either loses something that matters or makes the file bigger. Motion photos keep their video part intact. Anything copied unchanged is listed on the Files screen so you can see it happened on purpose \u2014 it is the app refusing to damage something, not a failure.
What happens if I uninstall, clear data, or change phones?

Your photos are unaffected. Optimised copies stay in Pictures/CloudSaver until your cloud app collects them, kept light copies stay in your gallery, and your cloud is untouched. CloudSaver\'s own history survives in a hidden file under Documents and Download, so reinstalling restores what it already knew and it does not redo work. On a new phone, install CloudSaver and copy that folder across, or use Save backup in Settings first.
What does freeing up space do, and can I get files back?

It is the one screen that can remove an original, and it only ever removes what you select. It lists files whose copies your cloud has provably collected, shows the proof for each one, and offers three modes \u2014 keep a light copy in your gallery, remove the original entirely, or just clear the copies waiting on your phone. Removed files go to your gallery trash, where Android keeps them for 30 days, and the Recently freed up screen lists every batch with a Restore button. If you choose the light-copy mode, the copies live in the Pictures/Light copies album \u2014 keep that album out of your cloud app\'s backup, because every file there already reached your cloud once and backing the album up would store it twice.

Nothing, from CloudSaver. The internet permission is removed from the app itself, so there is no code path that could send anything anywhere \u2014 not analytics, not crash reports, not your photos. All the network traffic you will see is your own cloud app uploading the folder, exactly as it would for any other folder. You can check this yourself in Android\'s app info screen, where CloudSaver has no network permission to grant or deny.
Why is there an Optimise now button if everything is automatic?

The schedule waits for good moments \u2014 charging, screen off, the day\u2019s allowance. The button skips the waiting, never the safety limits: it will not run when the phone is too hot, the battery is under 15%, or free space is below the reserve. The run is listed in Activity as \u201cStarted by you\u201d.
What are the .cloudsaver folders in Download and Documents?

They hold one small text file each: a list of file names, dates, sizes and short codes \u2014 never photos. It lets a reinstall pick up where you left off, and it is rewritten every day. Deleting them is safe: the app recreates them within a day. Only deleting every copy and then reinstalling loses the history \u2014 your originals and your cloud are unaffected either way. You never have to create this history yourself: it writes itself once a day, and a reinstall reads it back on its own. The Backup and restore buttons in Settings exist only for an extra copy you keep somewhere else, like a computer.
Where do the “Recommended for this phone” figures come from?

From this phone, measured on the spot: how much storage it has in total, and how much of it is free right now. A 64 GB phone and a 512 GB phone should not hold back the same headroom, so the app works out a reserve of about a twentieth of the phone (never under 1.5 GB), a daily limit that drops to the cautious figure on a small or nearly full phone, and a ceiling on its own working space of about a tenth of what is free, capped at 5 GB and never so low that the pipeline jams against it. Nothing is measured off the phone and no usage is sent anywhere. It is only ever an offer: the figure sits under the setting with a Use recommended button, your own value is never overwritten, and the line turns into a warning only when what is stored has drifted more than three times away from it.
Can the smaller copy stay in the same album instead of a new folder?

Yes. In Free up space, choose “Replace with light copy” and turn on “Keep it in the same album”. The optimised copy is then written into the album the original was in, under the original’s name and carrying its date, camera details and location — so your gallery timeline does not move and no extra folder appears. The copy is written and checked first; only then does Android ask you to confirm removing the original, and refusing leaves both untouched. Two honest caveats: a HEIC photo comes back as .jpg because that is what it was encoded to, and the file now in your album is the optimised version rather than the byte-for-byte original your cloud holds. CloudSaver recognises the replacement as the same photo, so it is never optimised a second time.
What happens if I have no cloud app installed?

CloudSaver still works, and still runs on its usual schedule: it optimises your photos and videos and puts the smaller copies in the Pictures/CloudSaver folder. What it cannot do is finish the journey, because nothing is there to collect them. So the copies stay in that folder, they count against the space you allowed the app to use, and once that space is full the app stops making more and says so on Home. No original is ever offered for removal either, because removal needs proof that a copy reached your cloud and there is no cloud to reach. Install a cloud app whenever you like and point it at that one folder \u2014 the waiting copies are picked up on its next backup, and nothing has to be redone.
Why does the Files list look empty when Free up space still finds things?

They answer different questions. Files is the work list: it shows what CloudSaver is going to optimise and what it already has, so it only ever covers the albums you ticked. Free up space is a cleaning tool for the phone as a whole \u2014 duplicates and your largest files are found in every album, ticked or not, because a duplicate wastes space wherever it sits. If Files looks empty, the usual reason is that no album is ticked yet; the list says so, and Settings has the album picker.
Android %1$s \u2014 removed files are deleted straight away instead of going to the gallery trash.
None \u2014 the app does not have the internet permission.

CloudSaver has no internet permission, so it cannot send anything anywhere. There is no account to create and no sign-in. There are no ads and no analytics of any kind. It also opts out of Android\u2019s own cloud backup, so the system never copies its records to your Google account either \u2014 a phone-to-phone transfer may still carry them, because that copy goes straight to your other phone.
Only the albums you included during setup. Albums you leave out are never read. You can change the list at any time in Settings.

File names, dates, sizes and a short code that identifies each file \u2014 the details needed to avoid doing the same work twice. Never your photos, and never thumbnails of them. It is all kept on the phone. A small backup of this list lives in the .cloudsaver folders under Download and Documents. That backup lets a reinstall pick up where you left off.
It never edits, moves or deletes your originals on its own. The only removals come from you, through Android\'s own confirmation. Nothing is deleted to make room for anything else.

No Android app can be made impossible to inspect, and anyone claiming otherwise is selling something. CloudSaver protects you by holding no secrets worth stealing and by checking that its own code has not been altered.
The app is provided as is, without warranty of any kind. It is a helper, not a backup service. Keep checking your cloud app yourself.

Light copies stay on this phone

These live in your gallery like any other photo. CloudSaver never optimises them again, never uploads them, and never removes one on its own. One thing to avoid: do not add the Light copies album to your cloud app\'s backup — every file here already reached your cloud once, and backing the album up would store it twice.
Keep this album out of your cloud app\'s backup — these files are already in your cloud.
Every place a file can disappear from, and what actually happens next. In every row, your originals are only ever removed by you.

If it was already confirmed as backed up, nothing happens — a disappearing copy is exactly what an upload looks like. If it was not yet confirmed, CloudSaver remakes the copy from your original and puts it back in the upload folder. If the same copy keeps vanishing before it is collected, the file is set aside and listed under Skipped instead of looping.
An original photo or video in your gallery

CloudSaver never deletes an original by itself, so this only happens by your hand or another app\'s. Anything already in your cloud stays there. If the file had not been optimised yet, there is simply nothing left to optimise, and the app stops counting it.
A kept light copy in Pictures/Light copies
That album belongs to you and CloudSaver never touches it. Removing a light copy only frees phone space — the full file is still in your cloud, and nothing is optimised or sent again.
The .cloudsaver history files in Download or Documents

Recreated within a day, automatically, with no chip and no alert. The history is only lost if every copy is deleted and the app is reinstalled before the next daily save — and even then your photos and your cloud are unaffected.
A file inside your cloud app

CloudSaver cannot see inside your cloud, so it does not notice — and it will not send the file again, because its record says the file was already delivered. Restore it from the cloud app\'s own trash. This is why the free-up screen asks you to open the cloud app and look before removing originals.
CloudSaver itself — uninstalled, or its data cleared

Nothing happens to your files: originals stay, copies stay in Pictures/CloudSaver until your cloud app collects them, kept light copies stay, and your cloud is untouched. On reinstall the app reads its daily history back and carries on where it stopped.
